title: What I trust
hook: Sariputta's lion's roar of confidence in the Buddha
carry: here is why I trust it

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first ruler, chosen by the people. Your line: freed by what you do. Today a great disciple makes a bold claim, and gets questioned for it.

She's the best doctor in the world. This is the greatest band that ever lived. People say things like that out of love, and it's usually more than they could prove. Sariputta, the disciple known for wisdom, comes to the Buddha at Nalanda and says something like it. Sir, I'm so confident in you that I believe there has never been, will never be, and is not now anyone who surpasses you in awakening. It's called a lion's roar. And the Buddha doesn't just smile and accept the compliment.
screen: `THE BEST IN THE WORLD.` → `SARIPUTTA'S LION'S ROAR.` → `THE BUDDHA DOESN'T JUST ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Sampasadaniya, the one that inspires confidence, the twenty-eighth. The Buddha answers with questions. Lofty words, Sariputta. Have you known the minds of all the Buddhas of the past? No, sir. Of all the Buddhas to come? No, sir. Of me, right now, so you could say exactly what my virtue and wisdom are? No, sir. Then why such a bold roar? It's a fair challenge, and Sariputta takes it honestly. He doesn't claim to know what he doesn't. He says: I know it by the way the teaching goes. The Blessed One taught me step by step, each stage finer than the last, and as I understood it, my confidence in the teacher grew. When the same conversation is told in the account of the last journey, Sariputta adds a picture. A king's frontier town has strong walls and only one gate, and a wise gatekeeper walks all the way around and finds no gap, not even one a cat could slip through. He doesn't need to count every creature; anything large enough to matter comes through the one gate. So too, every awakened one, past, future and present, passes through the same gate: letting go of the hindrances, establishing mindfulness, developing the factors of awakening. Back in the Sampasadaniya, he goes on to list, one by one, what he has found well taught. His confidence doesn't shrink. It changes shape: from I know everything to here is what I've checked, and here is why I trust it. In Pali the word is pasada: a clear, settled confidence, like water after the mud has sunk.
screen: `HAVE YOU KNOWN ALL THEIR MINDS?` · `NO, SIR. BUT I KNOW THE WAY.` · `ONE GATE, NO GAP FOR A CAT.` · `PASADA: CLEAR, SETTLED CONFIDENCE.` · then, large: `WHAT I TRUST.`

segments.voice: Name to yourself one thing you trust, a person, a practice, a teaching, a friendship, and ask the Buddha's question: what do I actually know about it? Then ask Sariputta's: what have I checked for myself? Let the confidence settle like muddy water going clear, and if it's still there, say quietly what you trust and why.
pasada. In DN 28 Sariputta's confidence is questioned, and he grounds it in what he has understood of the teaching, like a gatekeeper who knows his walls. Today's word.
Your line: here is why I trust it. Settled, like water gone clear. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists describe saddha, faith or confidence, as one of the five spiritual faculties, and many teachers explain it as trust that grows through testing the teaching in one's own practice.

original.note: Pali pasada: clarity, serene confidence. the root of sampasadaniya, inspiring confidence.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing without asking questions.
what it means: in DN 28 confidence is questioned, and rests on what has been checked.

what a scholar hears: in DN 28 Sariputta grounds his roar in the way the Dhamma goes (dhammanvaya); DN 16 and SN 47.12 tell the same exchange with the frontier-town simile, where the 'gate' is the abandoning of the hindrances, satipatthana and the bojjhangas.
recall: faith, trust, confidence in the path
a view, a way of seeing
guess: clear, settled confidence, checked for yourself
blind certainty that won't allow any questions
a formal vow of obedience to a teacher

chat.says: If you trust your teacher, shouldn't you just say they're the greatest ever?
options: Sariputta was asked what he knew, so he rooted his trust in what he'd understood.
Yes, big praise is the best proof of faith, so say it as loudly as you can.
Only if you've read their mind; otherwise you shouldn't trust them at all.
chat.meaning: The Buddha asked if Sariputta knew every Buddha's mind; he didn't, so he grounded his confidence in the teaching he'd understood step by step.

Sariputta.meaning: a leading disciple, known for his wisdom

Nalanda.meaning: a town where Sariputta made his lion's roar

Sampasadaniya.meaning: Long Discourse 28, the one that inspires confidence

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 47.12 (Nalanda Sutta) and Digha Nikaya 16, parallels with the frontier-town simile

notes: DN 28 paraphrased. The Buddha's questioning and the frontier-town simile appear at the start of DN 28 and in DN 16 / SN 47.12; confirm placement and the 'gap for a cat' detail.
Sariputta's roar is presented as a disciple's confidence in his own teacher, not as a comparison between traditions.
Pasada as 'like water after the mud has sunk' is an illustrative image, not from the sutta; confirm acceptability.

Reviewer: the gate line was changed so the simile points where the sutta points (all Buddhas, past, future and present, go through the same gate), not to Sariputta's personal step-by-step checking. The practice's 'what have I checked for myself' remains an application, not a sutta claim.

Editor review (y2 557-575): SERIOUS attribution fix. The frontier-town/gatekeeper simile was presented as DN 28's; as far as this reviewer can tell, DN 28 has Sariputta answer by 'the way the Dhamma goes' (the Buddha taught him stage by stage and his confidence grew), while the gatekeeper simile belongs to the DN 16 and SN 47.12 tellings. The teach now says so. Keeper: confirm DN 28 lacks the simile. Also cut 'Everyone has said something like it'.
